clue.text: Retired policemen succeeding in language group.

indicators.note: succeeding means coming after, so the policemen's letters follow the little word

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: retired here means drawn back, so the policemen's letters are read backwards

parts.note: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, plain-clothes police

explanation.surface: Ex-police officers do well in a group of languages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' means drawn back, not pensioned off; CID is Britain's plain-clothes detective branch.
explanation.definitionFit: Indic is the branch of Indo-European tongues spoken across the Indian subcontinent, such as Hindi and Bengali.

clue.text: Unwise to have one motorway force endlessly crossing it

parts.note: I is the roman numeral for one
M, as in M1, stands for motorway

indicators.note: crossing means going across, so the truncated force spans the little word
endlessly means without its last letter

parts.note: the police are a force
taken as written

explanation.surface: It would be foolish to have one police force patrolling a single motorway forever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' drops the force's last letter, and 'crossing' wraps what is left round the little word, giving POLITIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Impolitic means imprudent or ill-judged, not sensible.

clue.text: Split up first of the earthenware

indicators.note: in a down clue up means read from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: split is slang for leave quickly, so fled

indicators.note: first of means only the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Something cracked at the top of the pottery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Split' means ran off, not cracked; 'up' reverses it in this down entry, giving DELF, and 'first of' adds T.
explanation.definitionFit: Delft is tin-glazed pottery, originally from the Dutch town of the same name.

clue.text: It was linked with the aim of protecting soldiers

definitions.text: It was linked with the aim of protecting soldiers

parts.words: It was linked with the aim of protecting soldiers
parts.note: the armour of interlocking metal rings worn by medieval soldiers was literally linked together to protect them

explanation.surface: Something was associated with an aim to protect troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'linked' reads as associated, but means made of metal links.
explanation.definitionFit: It is medieval armour made of interlocking iron rings, worn to protect fighters.

clue.text: Soviet official given order by girl in vehicle

indicators.note: in signals that the order and the girl sit inside the vehicle

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
OM is the Order of Merit
miss is a girl or young woman

explanation.surface: A Soviet functionary is given orders by a young woman in a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' is an honour, the Order of Merit, not a command.
explanation.definitionFit: A commissar was a Communist Party official in the USSR, especially one in charge of political education.

clue.text: Like block, say, in area partitioned off

indicators.note: say signals that the word is spoken and written as it sounds

parts.note: a block is a cube shape, so cubical means like a block

explanation.surface: A block-like space is fenced off in a room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' turns 'cubical' into a word sounding the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A cubicle is a small enclosed compartment, such as a changing booth in a larger room.

clue.text: Greatest team embraced by mothers

indicators.note: embraced by means hugged, so one piece sits inside the others

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
mum is the British informal word for mother
XI, eleven, is a cricket or football team

explanation.surface: The best team gets hugs from the mums.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mothers' supplies two separate informal words; a team of eleven is written XI.
explanation.definitionFit: Maximum used as an adjective means the highest or largest possible.

clue.text: Mature monarch, for example, giving Cockney chap a turn

parts.note: a Cockney drops the h, so him becomes 'im
a go is a turn, as in 'your go'

explanation.surface: An adult king gives a Londoner his turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'monarch' is a butterfly, not a king. A Cockney is a working-class Londoner who drops initial h.
explanation.definitionFit: An imago is the final, adult stage of an insect, such as the full-grown butterfly.

clue.text: Lie in Procrustes' bed sometimes

definitions.meaning: an exaggeration or tall story, informal
Procrustes, in Greek myth, stretched short guests to fit his bed, so the bed acted as a rack that pulled people longer

explanation.surface: Lying down in Procrustes' bed now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lie' is a noun meaning a fib, not the act of lying down.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal word for a falsehood, and also something that elongates people, as the mythical robber's bed did to shorter guests.

clue.text: Bill's addition makes us one up

definitions.meaning: a clause added to a parliamentary bill or document
someone on horseback puts us one up, a mounted person being the 'one up' on a horse

explanation.surface: A clause attached to a law gives us an advantage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one up' suggests being ahead, but it means mounted on a horse, as racing speaks of a jockey being up.
explanation.definitionFit: A clause tacked on to legislation has this name, and so does a person on horseback.

clue.text: A queen wearing hat in shade of red

indicators.note: wearing means having something round you, so one piece sits inside the hat

parts.note: a pillbox is a small round brimless hat
R, for Regina, is the abbreviation for queen

explanation.surface: A queen in a red hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wearing' places A and R (Regina) inside PILLBOX; in this crossword container convention the hat goes round the queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Pillar-box red is the bright red of British postboxes, a named colour shade.

clue.text: In dry environment, beginning to crave bitter

indicators.note: environment means surroundings, so the dry word forms the setting round another letter

parts.note: arid means dry

indicators.note: beginning to means only the opening letter of the next word is used

explanation.surface: In a dry setting, the start of a craving for something bitter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to' takes C from crave, and 'environment' puts ARID round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrid describes a sharp, pungent taste or smell, close in sense to bitter.

clue.text: Language once spoken in school at Inverness

indicators.note: in signals that the answer is concealed inside the following words

explanation.surface: A dead language once heard in a Highland school.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across schooL AT INverness; 'in' points inside. Inverness is a city in the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin was the speech of ancient Rome and is now no longer spoken as a mother tongue.

clue.text: Dummy used to display scarf

definitions.meaning: a dummy is a rubber teat given to a baby to suck
a long woollen scarf, a sense now dated

explanation.surface: A shop dummy shows off a scarf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dummy' is the baby's pacifier, not a mannequin as the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a baby's pacifier is also called this, and it is likewise an old word for a long woollen neck wrap.

clue.text: Prepared to leave, having dined by river

parts.note: the Test is a river in Hampshire, England, famous for trout
ate means having dined

explanation.surface: Someone ready to set off after eating beside a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prepared to leave' means having made a will to leave property, not about to depart.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone testate has drawn up a valid will, so is ready to bequeath an estate.

clue.text: Scan Times frantically for meaning

indicators.note: frantically means wildly, so the letters of the words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A reader searches the newspaper in a frenzy to find out what something means.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frantically' rearranges SCAN TIMES.
explanation.definitionFit: Semantics is the study of sense in language, what words signify.

clue.text: Analgesic again almost left out of medicine bottle

indicators.note: almost means the word falls just short, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: more means again, as in 'do it once more'

indicators.note: out of signals the following letter being removed from the bottle

parts.note: a phial is a small bottle for medicine

explanation.surface: A painkiller, with some left over from the medicine bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims MORE to MOR; 'out of' takes L from PHIAL to leave PHIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Morphia is an older name for morphine, a powerful painkilling drug.

clue.text: Venerate American hero joining northern church

parts.note: Paul Revere is the American patriot famous for his midnight ride
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Honour an American hero who joins a church in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: CE is the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: To reverence is to treat with deep respect or worship.

clue.text: Relating to a period in the club

definitions.text: Relating to a period in the club

parts.words: Relating to a period in the club
parts.note: 'in the club' is British slang for pregnant, so this describes the months before a birth

explanation.surface: Something to do with time spent at a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the club' is British slang for expecting a baby, not membership of a club.
explanation.definitionFit: Antenatal means before birth, concerning pregnancy.

clue.text: Pet consuming a lot of fruit in Arthur's place

indicators.note: consuming means eating, so the pet takes the fruit inside it

parts.note: a cat is a pet

indicators.note: a lot of means most but not all, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a melon is a fruit

explanation.surface: A pet eats lots of fruit at King Arthur's castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lot of' drops the last letter, giving MELO; 'Arthur's place' is the legendary castle.
explanation.definitionFit: Camelot is the legendary court and castle of King Arthur.

clue.text: Glorious day and dramatic night

definitions.meaning: the Glorious ... is 12 August, when the British grouse-shooting season opens
... Night is a comedy by Shakespeare

explanation.surface: A splendid day and a theatrical evening.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Glorious' day is 12 August, the start of grouse shooting in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: This ordinal names both August's grouse-season opening day and Shakespeare's comedy about the eve of Epiphany.

clue.text: Young creature at all times hemmed in by obstruction

indicators.note: hemmed in by means surrounded by, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: let is an old word for obstruction, as in 'without let or hindrance'
ever means at all times, always

explanation.surface: A youngster is always fenced in by some barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: LET means obstruction in the legal phrase 'without let or hindrance'.
explanation.definitionFit: A leveret is a hare in its first year, a young animal.

clue.text: Form of service that gets GI truly involved

indicators.note: involved means tangled, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A church service that really engages an American soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' rearranges GI TRULY.
explanation.definitionFit: A liturgy is the set order of public worship in a church.

clue.text: Entrances adapted for emerging again

indicators.note: adapted means altered, so the letters of the word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Doorways remodelled for a revival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adapted' rearranges ENTRANCES.
explanation.definitionFit: Renascent means being reborn or reviving, coming into being once more.

clue.text: Extend 20% of readership with novel

indicators.note: the word has ten letters, so twenty percent is its first two

parts.note: novel means new

explanation.surface: Lengthen a subscription for a fifth of the readers with a book.
explanation.walkthrough: '20% of' takes the first two of the ten letters of readership, RE.
explanation.definitionFit: To renew a licence or subscription is to prolong it.

clue.text: Writers' not needed for modern record systems

definitions.text: Writers' not needed for modern record systems

parts.words: Writers' not needed for modern record systems
parts.note: pointed writing tools share their name with the needles of record players, which digital players no longer use

explanation.surface: Authors are surplus to the needs of modern filing systems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writers' are pointed writing implements, and 'record systems' are music players, not office files.
explanation.definitionFit: Styluses were ancient writing tools and are also gramophone needles, made obsolete by compact discs.

clue.text: Tree in Western circled by horse

indicators.note: circled by means surrounded, so one letter is placed within the horse

parts.note: a roan is a horse with a coat of mixed colours

explanation.surface: A tree in a cowboy film is ridden round by a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circled by' puts W inside ROAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The rowan, or mountain ash, is a tree with red berries.

clue.text: Risk forgetting composer's name

indicators.note: forgetting means leaving out, so a letter is dropped from the composer

parts.note: Richard Wagner was a German composer

explanation.surface: Gamble on not remembering the composer's name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forgetting' removes N from WAGNER.
explanation.definitionFit: A wager is a bet, money put at stake.

clue.text: Inquisitive about individual responsible for racket

indicators.note: about means around, so the inquisitive word goes round another letter

parts.note: nosy means inquisitive
I, the roman numeral one, stands for an individual

explanation.surface: A snooping person is the one behind the din.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts NOSY round I.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that makes a lot of din or loud commotion can be described as loud and clamorous.

clue.text: Sparred with man on board, say, for some time

indicators.note: say signals that the words are spoken, with the result written as it sounds

parts.note: sparred means fought, and the man on a chessboard is a knight

explanation.surface: Someone boxed with a chess piece for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' gives the sound of 'fought knight'; the knight is a chess piece. In British English the two sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortnight is two weeks, a period of days.

clue.text: Rugby player I throw over line in angry fashion

parts.note: Wasps is an English rugby union club, so one of its players is a Wasp

indicators.note: over here means placed round, so the throw word spans another letter

parts.note: shy means throw, as at a coconut shy

explanation.surface: A rugby player tosses the ball over the touchline in a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' puts SHY round L. Wasps is a London rugby union club.
explanation.definitionFit: Waspishly means irritably or with a sharp, spiteful manner.

clue.text: Recruit forsaken by English is rejected

indicators.note: is rejected means thrown back, so the combined letters are read backwards

parts.note: lorn is a poetic word for forsaken

explanation.surface: A recruit abandoned by the English is turned away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is rejected' turns LORNE backwards. 'Recruit' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrol is to sign up or register someone as a member, the same as recruiting.
